title: The fivefold completeness of the natural cannot stand if one degree is missing; and the five things the Lord makes known
reading:
If even one of the five aspects of the natural mind were missing, the whole could not stand. The natural is held together as one only because all five degrees are kept in their order; remove any one, and the structure collapses. Whatever the proprium produces in the natural — whatever rises up today on the face of the earth, in the flesh — is humbled in the end. It does not reach the height of the elevated states the Lord sets above it; it does not match their breadth or their length or their depth. The proprium's productions, from the smallest to the greatest, are at last swallowed up in the great sea of natural perception, taken back into the mass from which they came, because nothing the soul claims can stand on its own. Nothing endures apart from the power that bears the whole, apart from the divine going-forth that gives sign and order to the All, apart from his holy light. When the soul brings forth from itself in self-claiming, it has blasphemed against the wisdom that is the Lord's glory.

And to the rational the Lord makes five things known.

First, he informs the soul that it belongs to the kind of the light — that what it most truly is comes from him, not from itself.

Second, he loosens for the soul the understanding of the states it has passed through: how the degrees of formation actually exist, and likewise how the darkness exists — what self-claiming is, in what manner it stands. He teaches the soul to see both sides of itself.

Third, he proclaims the greatness of the light: how divine truth puts the proprium's claim to shame and prevails over it. The soul learns that the light is stronger than what had bound it.

Fourth, he teaches that the soul has come to the boundary of death — to the flesh, the outermost where self-love most operates — and that he himself brings the soul out by the upper gate of that lowest place, where before it had been sealed in.

Fifth, he shows that the proprium and its workings are bound at last with a great bond: those self-loving arrangements that habitually cover over the Good and the righteousness are themselves held fast, so that what hid the Lord's good cannot hide it any longer.
